title: Sex at Dawn: The Prehistoric Origins of Modern Sexuality
target_audience: Adults interested in human sexuality and relationships
Readers curious about evolutionary psychology and anthropology
Academics and students in social sciences
Individuals questioning conventional views on monogamy and relationships
core_themes: The evolutionary roots of human sexual behavior
Challenging the assumption that lifelong monogamy is 'natural' for humans
Prehistoric social structures and their impact on mating and pair-bonding
The influence of agriculture and civilization on sexual norms
Contrasting contemporary Western views on sexuality with those of hunter-gatherer societies
primary_purpose: To question conventional beliefs about the naturalness of monogamy for humans by exploring evidence from anthropology, primatology, and evolutionary biology, and to argue that human sexuality evolved to be far more communal and flexible than contemporary Western norms suggest.

structure_format.narrative_style: Engaging, provocative, and humorous; combines academic research with accessible language
structure_format.organization: Organized into thematic chapters interspersed with scientific analysis, historical overview, and case studies
features: References to current psychological and anthropological research

key_concepts_lessons: Human sexual instincts were shaped during the long pre-agricultural phase of our evolution.
Prehistoric hunter-gatherer societies tended to be more egalitarian and sexually promiscuous than subsequent agricultural societies.
Popular assumptions about universal sexual jealousy, male sexual possessiveness, and female fidelity are culturally and historically constructed.
The rise of agriculture led to property ownership and social structures that enforced sexual monogamy, in part to manage inheritance and lineage.
Understanding the evolutionary origins of human sexuality can help explain the widespread struggles with monogamy in modern societies.
notable_features: Challenges established dogmas in evolutionary psychology
Provocative arguments that have generated debate and controversy
cultural_historical_context: Released amidst growing discontent with traditional models of relationships and an increased interest in polyamory, open relationships, and alternative sexualities. Timed with broader discussions questioning marriage norms and the science behind human mating.
reception_impact: Bestseller in popular science and sexuality categories
Sparked widespread debate in both academic and lay audiences
Praised for its bold arguments and accessible style
Criticized by some evolutionary psychologists and anthropologists for selective evidence and overstatement
Cited in discussions about non-monogamy, polyamory, and relationship diversity
comparable_titles: The Ethical Slut by Dossie Easton and Janet Hardy
Why Is Sex Fun? by Jared Diamond
